sections.text: You learn how to spark interest, ask, explain and guide a group safely. Ten short topics with exercises.

glance.q: What do you do in the course?
glance.a: You learn about science education, visit a science event, plan your own science workshop and guide others to explore and try things out.

glance.q: How do you complete the course?
glance.a: You work through the five parts at your own pace during the school year. The key evidence is guiding a real science workshop or event.
About $28.5\,\text{h}$, planned as $23 \cdot 75\,\text{min}$. That is the total workload, not 23 lessons in a classroom.
With the induction. Read its first topic and start your portfolio with your starting point.

glance.q: What do I need to document?
glance.a: In your portfolio you record your exercises, what you observed on a visit, your workshop plan, the times you guided, your working time and your self-assessment.

intro: A LUMA tutor works as a science tutor: they plan science events and take part in them. LUMA comes from the Finnish words for natural sciences and mathematics, and technology belongs to it too.

The course is not tutoring in mathematics, physics or chemistry. Its subject is science education and science communication: how to get children, young people and other students excited about phenomena, asking questions and trying things out themselves.

LUMA tutor is Kiviruukki upper secondary school's own programme. It complements Ruukkilabra, where you study science yourself, and Ahjo Makerspace, where you build and make. As a LUMA tutor you take science to others.
hub.idea_text: Everyone can wonder, ask and explore, whatever their age, language or earlier knowledge. The tutor's job is to make that possible.
hub.path_lead: The course has five parts. Work through them in order, but the parts may overlap with the events of the school year: you can, for example, visit a science event while you are still in the induction.
goals: say what science education and science communication are and why they are needed
explain a scientific phenomenon with language and pictures that suit the audience
ask questions that make a participant think and try things out themselves
guide a group so that everyone gets to take part
plan, test and improve a hands-on science workshop
take care of safety as your role requires and know when to call an adult
work as part of an event's organising team and take responsibility for your share
assess your own work and develop it based on feedback
hub.workload_lead: The total workload of the course is about $38 \cdot 45\,\text{min} = 1\,710\,\text{min}$, or $28.5\,\text{h}$. That equals $22.8$ lessons of $75\,\text{min}$. For planning, the workload is rounded to $23 \cdot 75\,\text{min}$.
hub.workload_rounding: $23 \cdot 75\,\text{min} = 1\,725\,\text{min}$, or $28\,\text{h}\ 45\,\text{min}$. This is $15\,\text{min}$ more than the exact workload. The rounding is intentional.
workload_points: The workload is the student's total workload, not 23 separate contact lessons.
It includes the shared induction meetings, independent preparation, event visits, planning and testing the workshop, working at events, and the portfolio and self-assessment.
Events vary in length, so you log your actual working time in minutes on the [working time log](lumatutor-tyokalut.html#tyoaika).
There may be reasonable flexibility between the parts if you agree on it with the teacher. The total scope and the goals stay the same.
hub.requirements_lead: To pass, you need all six of these:
requirements: You take part in at least one suitable visit to a science event.
You plan and test a science workshop.
You take part in guiding a science workshop or science event in practice.
You document your participation and assess your work in a portfolio.
Your total workload matches the scope of the course.
hub.assessment_lead: The course is assessed as pass or fail. Filling the hours is not enough on its own: the teacher assesses your work and your portfolio in the following areas.

criteria.title: Guiding skills
criteria.text: You let the participants do things themselves, you ask before you tell, and you notice who is left out.

criteria.title: Preparation
criteria.text: You have tried the workshop in advance, the equipment is ready and you know what to do if something does not work.

criteria.title: Cooperation
criteria.text: You agree on tasks with the other tutors and the teacher and keep to what was agreed.

criteria.title: Responsibility
criteria.text: You follow the safety instructions, respect the participants and do not collect personal data about them.

criteria.title: Active participation
criteria.text: You are at the events for the whole agreed time and take on tasks on your own initiative.

criteria.title: Development and reflection
criteria.text: Your portfolio shows what you learned, what changed and what you would do differently next time.

hub.plan_note: The scope of the course, the split of the workload and the assessment model are a planning decision. They apply only once they have been confirmed in Kiviruukki upper secondary school's local curriculum.
hub.safety: The teacher is responsible for supervision and for organising safety. You are never alone the person responsible at an event for minors. No personal data is collected from the children who take part in the workshops: no names and no identifiable photos.
hub.links_lead: LUMA tutor's own task is science education, guiding, events and science communication. Other Kiviruukki studies give it content.

perehdy.title: Get ready: grow into a LUMA tutor
perehdy.lead: Ten short topics on how to spark interest, ask, explain and guide. Each has an exercise and an example situation.
how: You can do the induction on your own or in two or three shared meetings led by the teacher. Shared meetings are best for the exercises that need an audience.
The workload is about $3 \cdot 75\,\text{min}$. For each topic, write one insight and the exercise you did in your portfolio.

meetings.title: Meeting 1: The tutor's role
meetings.text: Get to know each other and the tutor's task. Practise starting a group and making sure everyone gets involved.

meetings.title: Meeting 2: Ask, explain, show
meetings.text: Everyone gives a two-minute science demonstration and gets feedback. Practise turning a ready answer into a question.

meetings.title: Meeting 3: For everyone, and safely
meetings.text: Go through safety and who is responsible for what. Try one workshop from the workshop bank within the group.

topics.title: What is a LUMA tutor and what do they do?
text: A LUMA tutor is an upper secondary student who gets others interested in science, mathematics and technology. They run workshops, help at events and show by their own example that science is interesting and belongs to everyone.

A tutor is not a teacher or a science show performer. Their most important task is to get the participants doing, asking and discovering things themselves. Younger children often find an upper secondary student easier to approach than an adult, and that is the tutor's strength.
points: A tutor guides, not lectures.
A tutor does not need to know everything: ”I don't know, let's find out together” is a good answer.
A tutor always works together with the teacher and the other tutors.

practice.title: Exercise: Me as a tutor
practice.text: Write three sentences in your portfolio: why you want to be a LUMA tutor, what your strength is and what you want to learn. This is the first part of the portfolio.

case.title: Example situation
case.text: A third-grader asks: ”Are you a teacher?” What do you answer, and how can your answer make the situation more relaxed?

topics.title: How do you get children and young people interested in science?
text: Interest starts when something surprises and the participant wants to know why. A good start is a phenomenon, not a definition: a bulb that lights with one wire but not another, or a sheet of paper that holds coins once you fold it.

Success keeps interest going. Plan the workshop so that the first success comes within a few minutes and a harder challenge only after that. Your own enthusiasm spreads: if you genuinely wonder, the participants wonder too.
points: Start with a phenomenon or a question, not an explanation.
First success quickly, the challenge after it.
Praise trying and a good question, not only the right answer.

practice.title: Exercise: The hook
practice.text: Invent a start for some phenomenon that lasts at most 30 seconds and raises a question. Try it on a friend: did they ask something?

case.title: Example situation
case.text: A lower secondary student says right at the start: ”Physics is boring.” How do you go on so that they get a chance to be surprised, without arguing with them?

topics.title: How do you guide a group?
text: Guiding a group starts before anyone touches the equipment. Introduce yourself, say briefly what you will do and agree on one clear signal for everyone to stop and listen, for example a raised hand.

Give instructions one step at a time and show them. Hand out the equipment only after the instructions, or no one will listen. Go round the groups, look at everyone and give each person a task: builder, measurer, recorder, presenter. The roles rotate.
points: One instruction at a time, show it and say it.
Equipment only after the instructions.
A role for everyone, and the roles rotate.
Agree on a stop signal right at the start.

practice.title: Exercise: Everyone in
practice.text: Guide a group of three to build a tower from ten sheets of paper. Rules: everyone touches the structure in turn, and you do not touch it at all. What did you notice?

case.title: Example situation
case.text: One participant does everything, and the other two watch. What do you say or do to change this without offending anyone?

topics.title: How do you ask good questions?
text: A question with one right word as its answer stops thinking. An open question starts it: ”What do you think will happen?”, ”What do you notice?”, ”How could you test it?”

When a participant asks you something, do not answer straight away. Turn the question back or suggest trying: ”Good question. What if we try?” Wait calmly for an answer. Silence often means someone is thinking.
points: An open question before the explanation.
Wait at least five seconds for an answer.
Turn the question into an experiment.
All the question cards are in the [toolkit](lumatutor-tyokalut.html#kysymyskortit).

practice.title: Exercise: From answer to question
practice.text: Turn these ready answers into questions that make the participant think for themselves: ”The bulb does not light because the circuit is not closed.” ”Folded paper holds more because it is stiffer.” ”The red film lets only red light through.”

case.title: Example situation
case.text: A participant asks: ”Why doesn't this work?” Write three questions that help them find the fault themselves.

topics.title: How do you explain difficult things clearly?
text: A good explanation starts from what the listener already knows. Use everyday words, comparisons and pictures. Say one thing at a time and check that the listener is still with you.

A comparison helps, but every comparison breaks down somewhere. Say so out loud: ”A circuit is a bit like water pipes, but electricity does not pour out of a wire if the wire breaks.” Avoid terms you cannot explain yourself without other terms.
points: Start from what the listener already knows.
One thing at a time, then a check.
A comparison and a picture, and say where the comparison breaks down.
You may use the proper terms once you have explained them.

practice.title: Exercise: For a primary pupil
practice.text: Explain a scientific phenomenon to a primary school pupil without difficult concepts, for example why the sky is blue or why ice floats. Write the explanation in at most five sentences and ask a friend to find a word in it that a 9-year-old would not understand.

case.title: Example situation
case.text: You are explaining a circuit, and a participant says: ”I don't get it.” What do you do next if the same explanation again does not help?

topics.title: How do you get participants to explore and try things themselves?
text: Exploring often goes like this: predict, try, observe, explain. When a participant first guesses what will happen, they watch the experiment more closely and remember the result better.
Give the participants a task with many solutions and keep your own hands in your pockets. A mistake is part of research: ”What did we learn from this?” is better than ”Wrong.”
points: Predict before trying.
Tasks that allow many solutions.
The tutor does not do it for the participant.
Ask what a mistake taught.

practice.title: Exercise: Predict first
practice.text: Choose a simple experiment, for example whether an orange floats with and without its peel. Write a prediction question for it, a one-sentence instruction for trying it, and a question with which the participant explains the result.

case.title: Example situation
case.text: A group wants you to show them the right solution straight away. How do you keep the exploring with them and still help them forward?

topics.title: What makes a good science demonstration?
text: A demonstration is a short show in which the audience sees a phenomenon. A good demonstration can be seen from the back row, lasts a few minutes, works reliably and leaves a question the audience wants answered.

Build the demonstration in three parts: a question or prediction, the show and a discussion. Rehearse it many times in advance and think about what you will do if it fails. A failure can also teach something when you say out loud what you think happened.
points: Visible to everyone, lasts a few minutes.
A question before the show, a discussion after it.
Rehearsed, with a backup plan ready.
The planning template is in the [toolkit](lumatutor-tyokalut.html#demonstraatio).

practice.title: Exercise: A two-minute demonstration
practice.text: Prepare a two-minute science demonstration with everyday equipment and give it to a group or film it for yourself. Time it. Ask for feedback on two things: could the phenomenon be seen, and did a question stay in mind?

case.title: Example situation
case.text: The demonstration fails, and the audience starts to giggle. What do you say to make the situation part of science?

topics.title: How do you take different learners and participants into account?
text: A group always has people of different ages, who learn in different ways and speak different languages. Someone is quick, someone needs more time, someone does not see or hear well, and someone is nervous. A good workshop works in many ways: by showing, saying, trying and with a picture.

Plan an easier and a harder version of every workshop. Speak clearly in short sentences, show as you speak, and check that the equipment can also be reached from a wheelchair. Do not assume anything about a participant from their appearance or their name.
points: Show and say, do not only say.
An easier and a harder version ready.
Clear language: short sentences, one thing at a time.
Space and equipment within everyone's reach.

practice.title: Exercise: Without words
practice.text: Guide a friend through a simple task, for example folding a paper plane, without speaking at all. What does this tell you about instructions for a participant whose language is different from yours?

case.title: Example situation
case.text: One participant is done in half the time and starts to disturb the others. What could you give them to do?

topics.title: How do you act safely and responsibly?
text: Safety is planned in advance. Every workshop card has safety instructions: read them and go through them with the teacher. The teacher is responsible for supervision, but you are responsible for following the instructions and for stopping the activity if something looks dangerous.

Responsibility also means respecting the participants. Do not collect names or other personal data from the participants, do not photograph anyone without permission, and tell the teacher at once if someone gets hurt or a situation worries you.
points: Read the workshop's safety instructions and go through them with the teacher.
You may, and must, stop the activity if something is dangerous.
No personal data, no photos without permission.
Tell the teacher at once about anything that worries you.
Use the [safety checklist](lumatutor-tyokalut.html#turvallisuus) before every workshop.

practice.title: Exercise: Spot the risks
practice.text: Choose one workshop from the workshop bank and find three things in it that could go wrong. For each, write how to prevent it and what you will do if it happens anyway.

case.title: Example situation
case.text: In the middle of a workshop, a participant puts a button cell in their mouth. What do you do at once, and whom do you tell?

topics.title: What is good science communication?
text: Science communication means telling people who are not experts in a field about research-based knowledge. Good science communication is true, understandable and interesting, and it also tells how the knowledge was gained and what is not yet known.

As a tutor you are a science communicator. Say where the knowledge comes from, separate an observation from an interpretation, do not exaggerate, and say plainly if you do not know. A reliable source is, for example, a research institute, a university or a textbook, not just a social media post.
points: True, understandable and interesting, in that order.
Say where the knowledge comes from.
Separate observation (what we saw) and interpretation (what it means).
”I don't know” is an honest answer.

practice.title: Exercise: One picture, one message
practice.text: Choose one graph or picture from a reliable source and write a title for it and two sentences that tell a lower secondary student what can be seen in it. Give the source.

case.title: Example situation
case.text: A participant says they saw a video claiming that climate change is a hoax. How do you talk with them respectfully and based on knowledge?

done: you have gone through all ten topics
you have done the exercise for each topic or done it in a shared meeting
you have given a two-minute science demonstration
your portfolio has your starting point and your main insights from the induction

tutustu.title: Visit science events
tutustu.lead: See how others do science education and collect ideas for your own workshop. Take part in at least one suitable science event.
why: As a LUMA tutor you do not only organise events. You also learn to look at how experienced science communicators and science educators do their work: how they start, what they ask and how they get the audience to try things.
On a visit you are an observer. You watch how it is done and how the audience reacts, not only the phenomena. No long report is needed: the aim is to collect thoughts and ideas for your own work.
tutustu.kinds_lead: A suitable event is one where the public hears about science or gets to try things themselves. Examples:
kinds: science days and open days at universities
other science events the teacher approves
tutustu.kinds_note: The list gives examples of kinds of events. They are not agreed visits or partnerships. Always check the timing and suitability of an event with the teacher first.

modes.title: Group visit
modes.text: The teacher arranges a visit for the whole tutor group. Agree in advance who observes what.

modes.title: Your own visit
modes.text: You visit an event on your own, for example at a weekend. Tell the teacher in advance where you are going and make sure the event is suitable.

modes.title: As an assistant
modes.text: You help a workshop leader at an event. You see the workshop from the inside, and this is often the best way to learn.

steps.title: Before
items: Agree on the visit with the teacher and check the event's programme.
Choose one or two things to observe in particular.
Print the [observation template](lumatutor-tyokalut.html#havainnointi) or copy it to your phone.

steps.title: During
items: Take part yourself, try things and listen.
Watch the audience: when do they get excited, and when does their attention drift?
Make short notes as soon as something gives you an idea.
Do not photograph people without permission. You may photograph equipment and set-ups if the organiser allows it.

steps.title: After
items: Complete the observation template on the same day.
Choose one idea to try in your own workshop.
Add your observations to the Visits to science events part of your portfolio and log the time you spent.

tutustu.observe_lead: Look at the event from the point of view of science communication and science education. Answer the six questions in a few sentences.
observe: How was the science made understandable?
How was the audience's interest sparked?
How did the participants get to try and explore things themselves?
What demonstrations or workshops were there at the event?
What could I use in my own science workshop?
tutustu.template_note: A ready template you can copy, download or print:
tutustu.time: A workload of about $4 \cdot 75\,\text{min}$ is set aside for visits and observation. This covers preparing, the event itself and writing up your observations. Agree with the teacher on whether travel time counts. Log the actual time in minutes.
done: you have taken part in at least one suitable science event
you have answered the six observation questions
you have chosen at least one idea for your own workshop
your observations are in the portfolio and the time is logged

suunnittele.title: Plan a workshop
suunnittele.lead: The workshop bank has ready science workshops that upper secondary students can run, for example for comprehensive school pupils. Choose one, adapt it or plan your own.
suunnittele.bank_lead: Every ready workshop is a complete guide: goals, equipment, safety, step-by-step timing, background and printable participant material. The ideas for development are ideas that have not yet been written out or tried.
suunnittele.ideas_lead: These workshops are waiting for a developer. You can take one as your own planning task: write it out with the planning template, test it and bring it to the teacher.
suunnittele.own_h: How to plan and test a workshop
suunnittele.own_lead: Use the [workshop planning template](lumatutor-tyokalut.html#suunnittelu). The ready workshops show what a finished plan looks like.

own_steps.title: Choose a phenomenon and an audience
own_steps.text: Which phenomenon interests you, and who is the workshop for? A primary pupil needs shorter steps and more doing than a lower secondary student.

own_steps.title: Write the goal in one sentence
own_steps.text: What can the participant do or notice after the workshop? For example: ”The participant notices that the bulb lights only when the circuit is closed.”

own_steps.title: Plan the hook
own_steps.text: Start with a phenomenon or a question that sparks curiosity in under a minute.

own_steps.title: Plan the activity
own_steps.text: A task where the participants predict, try and observe. First success within a few minutes, then a challenge.

own_steps.title: Write the questions and the closing
own_steps.text: Three good questions and a closing in which the participants say what they noticed.

own_steps.title: Make a safety plan and an equipment list
own_steps.text: Go through the [safety checklist](lumatutor-tyokalut.html#turvallisuus). Show the plan to the teacher before testing.

own_steps.title: Test
own_steps.text: Try the workshop first yourself and then with other tutors or friends. Time it and ask for feedback with the [feedback form](lumatutor-tyokalut.html#palaute).

own_steps.title: Improve
own_steps.text: Write in your portfolio what happened in the test and what you changed. Changing the plan after a test is the most important part of planning.

suunnittele.time: A workload of about $4 \cdot 75\,\text{min}$ is set aside for planning and testing. Taking a ready workshop into use takes less time than planning your own, so when you use a ready workshop, make it your own: add your own hook, your own differentiation or a new step.
suunnittele.add_h: Adding a new workshop to the bank
suunnittele.add: When a workshop you planned has been tested and the teacher has approved it, it can be added to the bank. In Ruukkilabra each workshop is its own file, so adding one needs no changes to the site's code.
done: you have a written workshop plan or an adapted ready workshop
you have tested the workshop at least once with others
you have changed the plan based on the test
the plan, the test results and the changes are in your portfolio

toteuta.title: Run it: guide others
toteuta.lead: You run science workshops and help organise science events. Guiding a real workshop or event is the key evidence in the course.
toteuta.kinds_lead: The events are agreed with the teacher during the school year. Possible events include, for example:
kinds: visits by lower secondary students to the upper secondary school
Kiviruukki upper secondary school's open days
science events planned by the students themselves
Kiviruukki's own STEAM and Makerspace events
toteuta.kinds_note: The list gives possible kinds of events. The teacher tells you which events are on offer this school year.
toteuta.peer_lead: Peer tutoring can be part of the course, but it is not its main content. It is agreed with the teacher. Examples:
peer: guiding experimental work in physics or chemistry
supporting students who are preparing for competitions
toteuta.peer_note: The same holds in peer tutoring as in workshops: guide the other person to think, do not do it for them. First ask what they have already tried.
toteuta.task_lead: Before every event, go through these six questions with the teacher and the other tutors. Write the answers on the [event preparation checklist](lumatutor-tyokalut.html#valmistelu).

task.q: What am I expected to do?
task.a: Your own role: for example lead tutor, assistant, equipment manager or host. You know when you need to be there and what you do in each step.
You read the workshop card, try the workshop yourself, rehearse the start out loud and find out what kind of group is coming.
You make an equipment list from the workshop card, set aside spares and check that everything works, the day before and just before the start.
You agree who guides, who assists, who is in charge of the equipment and who tidies up. The teacher is responsible for supervision and safety.
You go through the [safety checklist](lumatutor-tyokalut.html#turvallisuus), you know where the first aid kit is and whom to contact if something happens.
You log the event, your role and your working time, collect anonymous participant feedback and fill in the tutor's self-assessment on the same day.

roles.title: Lead tutor
roles.text: Starts and ends the workshop, gives the instructions and keeps to the timetable.

roles.title: Assistant
roles.text: Goes round the groups, helps those who are stuck and notices who needs support.

roles.title: Equipment manager
roles.text: Prepares and hands out the equipment, keeps the spare parts safe and is in charge of tidying up.

roles.title: Host
roles.text: Welcomes the group, shows them around and takes care of moving from place to place.

toteuta.roles_note: The roles change from event to event. If the events make it possible, everyone gets to try the lead tutor role at least once.
responsibility: The teacher is responsible for proper supervision of the activity and for organising safety.
You are never alone the person responsible at an event for minors. The group's own teacher or another responsible adult is always there.
No personal data is collected from the participants. Feedback is anonymous, and identifiable photos are not taken or published without permission, following the school's practice.
toteuta.time: A workload of about $9 \cdot 75\,\text{min}$ is set aside for preparing and running events. This could be, for example, two or three events with their preparation, or several short workshops. For each event, log the time spent on preparing and on guiding separately.
done: you have taken part in guiding at least one real science workshop or science event
you have practised the lead tutor role, if the events make it possible (agree on this with the teacher)
for every event, your role, working time, feedback and self-assessment are recorded

arvioi.title: Assess and hand in
arvioi.lead: The tutor portfolio shows what you did and what you learned. With it you follow your progress throughout the school year and show your skills.
arvioi.portfolio_lead: The portfolio has six parts. Fill it in as you go, not only at the end. Short, honest answers are better than long, general ones.
arvioi.portfolio_template: The whole portfolio is one [portfolio template](lumatutor-tyokalut.html#portfolio) that you can copy into your own file.

arvioi.time_lead: Log every work session: the day, what you did, which part it belongs to and how many minutes it took. At the end, add up the totals by part.
arvioi.self_lead: After every event, assess your work with the [tutor's self-assessment template](lumatutor-tyokalut.html#itsearviointi). At the end you assess your development over the whole course using the same areas the teacher uses to assess completion:
return: Hand in your portfolio and your working time log in the learning environment the school names separately. Ruukkilabra does not save anything you write: make the portfolio in your own file.
After handing in, you have a short feedback talk with the teacher. You go through the portfolio, the events and your self-assessment, and the teacher explains the grounds for the assessment.
check: all six parts of the portfolio have answers
the working time log is added up
every event has a role, working time and self-assessment
the portfolio has no participants' names or other personal data

tyokalut.title: Tutor's toolkit
tyokalut.lead: Templates and checklists for every stage of the course. They are made to be used directly at real events.
tyokalut.how: Every template can be copied into your own file, downloaded as a text file or printed. The Print button prints only that template. Nothing is saved in Ruukkilabra.

templates.title: Event preparation checklist
templates.use: A week before the event, the day before and just before the start.
blocks: [ ] The workshop is chosen and the workshop card read.
[ ] I have tried the workshop myself.
[ ] The equipment list is made and missing equipment ordered or borrowed.
[ ] The safety checklist has been gone through with the teacher.
[ ] The room is booked and I know where it is.
[ ] The equipment is counted and tested, spares included.
[ ] The start has been rehearsed out loud.
[ ] The timetable is clear to all tutors.
[ ] The equipment is in place and will be handed out only after the instructions.
[ ] I know where the first aid kit and the emergency exits are.
[ ] I know whom to contact if something happens.
[ ] The room is tidied and the equipment returned.
[ ] Working time and self-assessment are logged.

templates.title: Safety checklist
templates.use: Before every workshop, together with the teacher.
blocks: [ ] The teacher in charge or another responsible adult is there the whole time.
[ ] I know where the first aid kit and the emergency exits are.
[ ] Walkways are clear, and there are no cables or things on the floor.
[ ] The equipment suits the participants' age.
[ ] Participants have been asked about allergies if food, latex or another allergen is used.
[ ] No personal data is collected from participants, and they are not photographed without permission.
[ ] Only batteries or low voltage are used, never mains electricity.
[ ] Button cells are out of children's reach.
[ ] Participants are told not to short-circuit a battery: the wire can get hot.
[ ] Broken, leaking or hot batteries are taken out of use at once.
[ ] Only substances the teacher has approved. The safety data has been read.
[ ] Safety glasses are worn when a substance can splash.
[ ] A wet floor is dried at once.
[ ] Sharp tools only under guidance, not for young children.
[ ] No one looks straight at the sun or a bright lamp.
[ ] Lamps that get hot are placed where no one touches them.
[ ] I stop the activity and call the responsible adult at once.
[ ] If a child may have swallowed a button cell or a magnet, call 112 at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
[ ] I tell the teacher what happened on the same day.

templates.title: Cards of good guiding questions
templates.use: Print, cut out the cards and keep them with you in the workshop.
blocks: - What is strange or surprising here?
- What would you like to know about this?
- What do you think will happen if…?
- What do you change, and what stays the same?
- What happens if you do it differently?
- Did someone else notice something different?
- Why do you think it happened like that?
- How would you explain this to a friend?
- Where in everyday life do you see the same phenomenon?
- What was the most surprising thing today?
- Which part works and which does not?
- What if we try one change at a time?
